summary: Intermittent 401/403: JWT 'nbf' in milliseconds causes token rejected by private auth-proxy
description:
Issue summary:
Users at Acadia report intermittent 401/403 when accessing the private Console and calling admin APIs. Failures are transient — some sign-ins work immediately, others are rejected with 'token not yet valid' errors. This started after an IdP update rolled out by the customer on 2026-03-09.

Impact:
- Console login failures for administrators and CI jobs (affects deployments and deployments health checks)
- API calls to admin endpoints returning 401/403 intermittently, causing automated sync failures
- Customer on Private deployment (prod/us-west).

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Authenticate via customer IdP (Azure AD federation configured via private identity-bridge).
2) Exchange SAML->JWT through our bridge and call /v1/admin/ routes with returned token.
3) Some tokens are accepted; others return 401 with log: 'jwt validation failed: token not yet valid (nbf)'.

Observed behavior:
- Auth-proxy rejects JWTs with 'nbf' claim even when issued seconds earlier.
- Token payloads show 'nbf' values that look like epoch milliseconds (e.g. 1678828800000) rather than seconds (e.g. 1678828800).

Expected behavior:
- Auth validation should accept nbf values in seconds, or normalize millisecond timestamps emitted by some IdPs after SAML->JWT translation.
steps_to_reproduce: See the description steps. Reproducible with the customer's IdP token exchange; reproduced in our staging identity-bridge by replaying the SAML response they provided.
investigation_notes:
Initial triage: reproduced locally by replaying SAML-to-JWT mapping. Decoded JWTs show 'nbf' and 'iat' in millisecond precision. Our token validation path (auth-proxy) performs integer comparison assuming seconds. Because milliseconds values (1.6e12) >> time.time() (1.6e9), tokens are treated as 'not yet valid'.

Hypothesis: customer IdP or our SAML->JWT mapping recently started emitting epoch millis (breaking assumption). Change likely introduced in customer's IdP mapping or a new library version in identity-bridge.

Supporting evidence:
- Two tokens captured side-by-side: one with nbf in seconds (accepted) and one with nbf in millis (rejected).
- No clock skew evident on customer side (NTP consistent).
- Audit of identity-bridge logs shows no normalization step after SAML translation.

Next steps taken:
- Created PR to normalize numeric time claims (nbf, iat, exp) to seconds when values look like milliseconds. (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/9876)
- Added unit tests and a canary deployment to private us-west auth-proxy and identity-bridge.
- Requested customer to temporarily revert the IdP mapping that started emitting millis as a short-term mitigation.
workaround: Temporary: ask IdP admin to change SAML-to-JWT mapping to emit epoch seconds, or apply a temporary translation script in the identity-bridge config. We provided a one-line jq snippet to normalize claims for their ops team. As a short-term server-side workaround, we deployed a canary build that normalizes numeric claims if values appear to be in milliseconds.
resolution:
Patch merged and rolled out: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/9876. Canary passed for 24h in prod/us-west, then staged rollout to all private auth-proxies. Customer re-authenticated and reported no further 401/403s. Follow-ups: add a token-validation regression test to CI, document claim normalization in private deployment runbook, and notify on-boarding docs to handle millisecond tokens.

Closure notes: root cause was mismatch in expected epoch unit between our validator and certain IdP mappings. Deployed fix normalizes numeric time claims and includes telemetry to catch similar regressions in the future.
related_documents: Confluence runbook updated: https://confluence.redwood.ai/runbooks/auth-token-validation; Postmortem ticket INT-445 created for internal tracking.
